title: Vasquez assigns the moral-certainty view to Soto, Vega, and Tapper
source_text: XVIII. Hanc sententiam Vasquez Disput. modo citatae cap. 8. tribuit Dominico Soto, Andreae de Vega, & Ruardo Tappero. Et revera Tapperus ille ad Art. 9. Lovan. de praesenti quaestione disserens, In hoc, inquit, omnes Scholastici conveniunt, quod omnimoda certitudo gratiae a nobis haberi non potest, sed probabiliter eam assequi licet per signa, atque hoc sunt certiora quo clariora & manifestiora. Aliquando autem tam aperta sunt, ut nulla formido, nulla vacillatio sit conjuncta hujusmodi cognitioni. Et pag. sequenti, postquam proposuit tanquam quaestionem problematicam, & utrinque probabiliter disputabilem, An multo tempore in vitae sanctimonia exercitati, imo & poenitentes, sine revelatione Dei, ex signis, Scripturarum testimoniis, & experimentis visitationum Spiritus Sancti, certitudinem habere possint sine temeritate, justaque ratione, non quidem infallibilem, sed quae sit sine metu & formidinem, ne fortassis ita non sit sicut arbitrantur, hoc est, se gratiam non habeant: satis indicat quo inclinat ipse, addens, fieri posse quod efficacissima habeantur argumenta pro praesentia gratiae, & nulla occurrat causa verisimilis dubitandi, vel formidandi.
pass_a_gloss: Vasquez in the Disputation just cited, chapter 8, attributes this opinion to Dominicus Soto, Andreas de Vega, and Ruardus Tapper. And indeed that Tapper, discussing the present question at Louvain Article 9, says: In this all the Scholastics agree, that an all-sided certainty of grace cannot be had by us, but we may attain it probably by signs, and these are more certain the clearer and more manifest they are. But sometimes they are so open that no fear, no vacillation is joined to knowledge of this sort. And on the following page, after he has proposed as a problematic question, and probably disputable on both sides, Whether those long exercised in holiness of life, and even penitents, without God’s revelation, from signs, testimonies of the Scriptures, and experiences of the visitations of the Holy Spirit, can have certainty without rashness and with just reason—not indeed infallible, but such as is without dread and fear lest perhaps it not be as they think, that is, that they do not have grace—he sufficiently indicates where he himself inclines, adding that it can happen that most efficacious arguments are had for the presence of grace, and no likely cause of doubting or fearing occurs.
pass_b_english: Vasquez ties the moral-certainty line to Soto, Vega, and Tapper.
Tapper allows that clear spiritual signs can yield fearless though not infallible certainty of present grace.
